title: XYZ-forge — The Releases Ledger, its Derived Views, and the Push Guard
sources: ARCHITECTURE.md — 'The Ledger and its Derived Views' (landed in PR #483)
ARCHITECTURE.md — 'The Roadmap View Pipeline and its Push Guard' (landed in PR #485)
legend_note: Solid = synchronous call or unconditional write. Dotted = data read/dump. Dashed = an out-of-band signal (stderr). The one edge worth tracing is 'dropped-row warning' into the push guard: a dropped row renders to nothing, so byte-comparison drift detection cannot see it, and the guard reads the renderer's own stderr report instead.

groups.label: Write entry points — CLI verbs only
Derived views at the repo root
Write paths that refresh a view

nodes.label: releases.db
nodes.description: The source of truth for this repo's roadmap and release ledger. Never hand-edited: every mutation goes through a releases_app.py CLI verb.

nodes.label: releases.sql
nodes.description: The dump of releases.db, and the surface git actually merges. GID keying makes INSERT-only tables union cleanly; roadmap_items is edited in place, so a same-GID collision there is a real content conflict, not a dedupe.

nodes.label: releases_app.py
nodes.description: The single sanctioned write path into the ledger. Also calls refresh_preview() after a DB write, which is one of the four consumers subject to the adoption gate.

nodes.label: export_timeline.py
nodes.description: Renders the two HTML views. Both are adopted-by-presence, so this runs only when its target file already exists at the repo root.

nodes.label: utils/roadmap-dashboard.sh
nodes.description: Reads roadmap_items via a flat JSON SELECT and parses each row's raw_text. Runs the full render before its mode branch, so it emits the dropped-row warning in BOTH modes — which is what makes --check usable as a signal source and not just a comparator.

nodes.label: utils/leaderboard.sh
nodes.description: Renders LEADERBOARD.md. Adopted-by-presence.

nodes.label: adopted by presence?
nodes.tech: does the file already exist at the repo root?
nodes.description: The rule that makes a view addable and removable without editing a single consumer. A repo that never baked a view — a fixture, a fresh clone, a vendored .xyz/ install — is a silent no-op, not an error. An adoption rule enforced by four consumers out of six is not an adoption rule; GH-474 closed the two that leaked.

nodes.label: ROADMAP-DASHBOARD.md (retired)
nodes.description: Retired in GH-567. Previously required; now excised along with the push guard to eliminate merge churn. Roadmap inspection is on-demand via releases_app.py roadmap list.

nodes.label: LEADERBOARD.md
nodes.description: Opt-in. Delete it and every consumer stops refreshing it; run its generator and commit the result and every consumer resumes.

nodes.label: RELEASES-PREVIEW.html
nodes.description: Opt-in. The view wave_reconcile.py used to resurrect within a day of any un-adoption, before GH-474 presence-gated that call.

nodes.label: LEADERBOARD.html
nodes.description: Opt-in.

nodes.label: wave_reconcile.py
nodes.tech: Python · runs after every merged PR
nodes.description: GH-474 leak #1: refreshed RELEASES-PREVIEW.html unconditionally. Now presence-gated. Pinned by test/gh202-wave-reconcile-issue-state.sh, whose stub exporter WRITES the artifact when invoked — so 'absent afterwards' proves the step did not run.

nodes.label: releases-merge-resolve.sh
nodes.tech: bash · the sanctioned ledger merge path
nodes.description: GH-474 leak #2: treated every unmerged view as 'take either side and regenerate', which restores a file deleted on one side. Working-tree presence cannot detect this — during a delete/modify the surviving copy is sitting right there, so a -f test reports 'adopted'. Now reads both commits and honours the deletion.

nodes.label: express.py / jog_run.py
nodes.tech: Python · stages views into a lane commit
nodes.description: Presence-gated like the rest.

nodes.label: dropped-row warning
nodes.description: The signal that carries what drift detection structurally cannot see. It travels on stderr rather than as a new exit code because --check's exit contract is load-bearing for four other test suites. Two shapes share the matched prefix: unparseable rows, and rows under an unrecognised section heading.

nodes.label: githooks/pre-push
nodes.description: Entry point for the push gate. Classifies the push range and dispatches the staleness guard.

nodes.label: dashboard-staleness-guard.sh
nodes.tech: bash · refuses on drift OR on a dropped row
nodes.description: Fires when a push range writes the ledger but not the view. Keeps the renderer's stderr with '2>&1 >/dev/null' — order matters — and refuses on either signal. Before GH-474 it discarded that stderr and inferred the same fact from TABLE NAMES in the releases.sql diff: a hand-maintained allowlist that went short twice and left eight dump tables unclassified. Reading the renderer's own report cannot go short, because an unknown table is no longer a question the guard asks.

nodes.label: git archive projection
nodes.tech: private tmp root, pinned to local_sha
nodes.description: The guard renders from a commit-pinned projection, never the working tree, so uncommitted edits cannot change the verdict. Fails CLOSED: a projection that cannot run the renderer is treated as drift.

nodes.label: utils/py/router_audit.py
nodes.description: Validates ROUTER.md structure. Under GH-567, no longer requires ROADMAP-DASHBOARD.md; routes startup directly to releases_app.py roadmap list.

nodes.label: 4 suites on --check's exit
nodes.tech: 3 downstream: gh269-roadmap-retired · gh280-jog-marathon-adapter (2 sites) · gh57-live-merge-resolve — plus the renderer's own suite: roadmap-dashboard
nodes.description: Four suites treat a non-zero --check as failure. Three are downstream consumers that merely borrow the exit contract; the fourth, test/roadmap-dashboard.sh, is the renderer's own suite and tests that contract head-on — its case 4 mutates the artifact to prove --check ACTUALLY fails on drift, which is what makes the other three's reliance on it meaningful. Together they are why the dropped-row signal travels on stderr rather than as a new exit code: a new code would have broken all four.
